newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A -- Fiscal policy, budget gap Part V.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A -- Fiscal policy, budget gap Part V.

text.p: Following are excerpts from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's question-and-answer session the Senate Banking Committee with after the second day of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before .

Sen. Hagel (R-Nebraska)- "Especially in light of our ongoing tax and budget negotiations ... I'd ask you, if you would elaborate a little bit, especially on the fiscal (and) structural policies we're going to have to deal with ... on what you see ahead."

Greenspan: "One thing, I think, everybody agrees on is that the shock to the fiscal structure as we move towards 2010 and as the very dramatic rise in the birth rate just after the end of World War II begins to feed into the various programs which relate to the elderly ... that has very major effects as we look at both Social Security and Medicaid programs.

"We see a very large set of pressures impacting on the federal budget ... And I think that's why I obviously strongly support efforts to move towards a balanced budget, hopefully a surplus in the short run.

"It strikes me that in the context of reviewing budget policy, even in the short-run, that that issue be in the back of everybody's mind, knowing that there is a path there which is going to have to be, somehow, addressed.
"It's important to recognize that after 2002 the deficit starts to go up again and becomes a significant problem as we move into the second decade of the 21st century."
Senator: "We've had some times ... but while we're enjoying this strong economy today is there something we should be concerned about or at least planning for the downside of tomorrow?"

Greenspan: "We recognize ... that while things are doing exceptionally well today that we can't assume that that is going to happen indefinitely. And as a consequence, because we see such exceptional value ... in this expansion we think it's incumbent upon us, as we've discussed over the years, to remember that policy from the central bank doesn't impact the economy and price until a year or so after we implement it.
"So we're continuously focusing on the longer-term.
